newsitem.title: UK: Major denies he plans more "Eurosceptic" line.
newsitem.headline: Major denies he plans more "Eurosceptic" line.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Tuesday dismissed press reports that he was about to switch tack on the key issue of a European single currency which divides his Conservative Party.
"I have read the stories in the media over the last few days and most deserve the Booker Prize for Fiction," Major told journalists.

Reports in British newspapers this week have suggested Major might be about effectively to rule out Britain joining a single currency in the next five years if the Conservatives win an upcoming general election.

Finance minister Kenneth Clarke said on Monday such a move would be "senseless", but so-called Eurosceptic members of the party argue it could be the key to giving the Conservatives a fighting chance of winning the forthcoming general election.
Major has attempted to stop the wrangling in the party over the single currency with a wait-and-see policy, claiming the decision should not be made this side of a general election due by May 22.
He said on Tuesday that the issue had been examined by the cabinet again last week, adding: "Nothing has changed."
A row over Europe is the last thing Major needs given the Conservatives' already deep unpopularity.
A poll in the Guardian newspaper on Tuesday suggested last week's budget had only made matters worse, despite a one penny cut in the standard rate of income tax.
The poll by the ICM group showed the gap between the Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party had widened by six points in the past month to Labour 19 points ahead.

"We have to be cautious about drawing conclusions from a single poll," said one elections expert. "But if this trend is confirmed (by other polls), it is hard to see how the Tories (Conservatives) can hope to stay in power."

John Redwood, the Eurosceptic former cabinet minister who last year challenged Major for the party leadership, earlier told the BBC if Major chose to rule out jettisoning the pound, a clear majority of his cabinet would back him.
"The question is whether he judges that right now and whether he wishes to take that to cabinet," Redwood said.
Pro-European Conservative MP Quentin Davies made it clear Major would encounter fierce opposition from his side of the party if he came off the fence against a single currency.

"It would be completely crazy and contrary to the national interest to throw away our option to join the single currency. The British people would not respect a government that did such an irresponsible thing," he said.
Major said Clarke had this week negotiated assurances from fellow EU finance ministers that British economic policy would not be constrained if it stayed with the pound sterling.
"He (Clarke) told the House (of Commons) what he was going to achieve and he achieved it," Major said.
Labour, trying to play down its reputation as a tax-and-spend party, plans to abstain in the parliamentary vote on Clarke's budget scheduled for 2200 GMT on Tuesday.
But the party is looking forward to a December 12 by-election in the rock-solid Labour seat of Barnsley East which is certain to end Major's overall parliamentary majority.
That, Labour believes, will give it a chance to harry the Conservatives in parliament and maybe force an early election.
